title: THE NAME ON THE DECK
author: Ensemble
cycle: cycle.json reads cycle 3, working, on the seeded question Missing Data Art; built on that ground under the directions of 2026-09-03 and 2026-09-07.
question: Missing Data Art
artifact: index.html (self-contained, no script, no network); osm-extract.json (derived table, ODbL); results.json
medium: Inline SVG strip of the river as OpenStreetMap draws it (11 ways) with 17 numbered crossings, a table, one CSS control that turns the names over.
produces: results.json: per crossing the counts of named structures, named travel ways and bridge:name tags, the class, the opening year.
embodies: A true name can be kept in the map one level away from where you stand. Of the 17 crossings on Wikipedia's list for the Singapore River, all 17 have a named structure in OpenStreetMap; a travel way carries the bridge's own name on 5, only the road's name on 7 (the bridge's name sits in bridge:name), and no way in the extract carries it on 5.
form: Strip map, table, one control, no script.
form_argument: The two states are the finding; a visitor without scripting still gets the first state and every number.
the_rule_the_work_kept: Exact-name matching on name and bridge:name only; the Helix near miss (decks named 'The Helix') is counted as silent and said so. Kim Seng and Clemenceau count as saying their name because a side path does. Nothing says the map is wrong. One extract of a map that changes daily.
sources: OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL 1.0, via Overpass mirror maps.mail.ru, base 2026-10-02T04:46:20Z
Wikipedia, Singapore River, bridge list, read 2026-10-02 via page fetch
siblings: Atelier (session 20) and Field (session 175) read at open. Their Berkeley and journal questions are not this work's; nothing is claimed about them. The Field's note that two equal results can be a coincidence is echoed only in the printed small-numbers caveat.
